title: CoLLMLight: Cooperative Large Language Model Agents for Network-Wide Traffic Signal Control
one_liner: Traffic signals at intersections learn to coordinate across a whole network by having each signal's reasoning process run asynchronously and feed guidance back to the real-time decisions.
lead: Traffic in a city flows through many intersections, and each intersection's signal decisions ripple across the whole network. Most LLM agents treat each intersection in isolation, deciding its signal timing without considering what neighboring intersections need. CoLLMLight runs a separate reasoning process for each intersection that thinks about neighboring traffic patterns asynchronously—without blocking real-time decisions—and caches guidance that shapes the actual signal timing. This lets agents cooperate across the network while keeping decisions fast.

problem.h2: Treating each intersection like an island
paras: Consider a city block with five intersections. If each intersection's signal decides its own timing in isolation—only looking at its own queue length—cars pile up at one intersection because the upstream signal is green when it should be red, and nobody told it to change. Traffic is a network: a decision at intersection A affects intersection B two blocks away.

A beginner might try: run an LLM at each intersection, feed it the local queue length, and let it decide when to switch the light. This works okay for one isolated junction, but in a real network, the LLM at intersection A has no idea that intersection B is about to flood it with cars. By the time A sees the incoming cars, it is too late to prepare.

callout.html: Each intersection makes decisions alone without knowing what other intersections need, so traffic cannot be optimized across the whole city.

steps.b: Each intersection runs two processes in parallel.
steps.text: One makes real-time signal decisions in milliseconds; the other thinks deeply about cooperation without rushing.

steps.b: The reasoning process looks at neighboring intersections.
steps.text: It predicts how many cars will arrive from neighbors and what timing would reduce waiting because the next light choice can reserve time for those incoming cars.

steps.b: Reasoning output is cached as guidance.
steps.text: The slow thinking result is stored and reused for the next few seconds, not re-computed on every decision.

steps.b: Real-time decisions read the cached guidance.
steps.text: When the light must switch right now, the fast decision-maker checks: does my neighbor need me to stay green or flip to red?

steps.b: Training adjusts which intersections listen to which neighbors.
steps.text: Reinforcement learning rewards network-wide smooth flow and penalizes reasoning that takes too long or uses too much computation.

paras: The paper moves the reasoning process out of the critical path. Instead of deciding on the fly, it thinks asynchronously and feeds guidance into real-time decisions. This lets intersections reason deeply about neighbors without blocking millisecond-level signal timing.

hidden.h2: The hidden quantity: cooperation guidance quality
hidden.name: cooperation guidance quality
paras: The paper measures an invisible quantity: how good is the guidance that one intersection's reasoning produces for its neighbors? Good guidance steers the real-time decision maker toward timing that helps the whole network because it describes near-future cars before they physically arrive. Bad guidance is either wrong predictions of neighbor traffic, or suggestions that contradict the urgent local need.

The paper estimates this by running reinforcement learning: it gives rewards when the whole network waits less (cars spend less time in queues), and penalties when the reasoning process wastes computation or text generation. Over time, the LLM learns which neighbors matter and what guidance actually moves traffic.

heat.caption: Darker means more important to cooperation guidance quality. Highlighted cells drive the final signal decision.

reads.html: When intersection A thinks asynchronously, it predicts: in three seconds, intersection B will have 20 cars waiting. It sends that prediction to B as guidance. B's real-time decision then checks: should I give priority to those incoming cars? That prediction quality—how close to 20 actually arrive—is the cooperation guidance quality.

CoLLMLight optimizes guidance quality via reward signals in reinforcement learning. The reward includes network-wide throughput (fewer total vehicle wait seconds) and reasoning cost (token count + computation time). The LLM learns to send guidance only when it is confident and to stop reasoning when the benefit stops growing.

mechanism.h2: Why asynchronous reasoning + cached guidance work
paras: Real-time decisions must happen in milliseconds—the signal cannot wait for deep reasoning. But deep reasoning takes seconds. The trick is to run them in separate processes. The reasoning process thinks about the network constantly, updates its predictions of what neighbors will need, and caches those predictions. The real-time process reads the cache in milliseconds. Because the cache was computed while the reasoning process was not waiting for anything, the real-time process gets the benefit of deep thinking without the delay.

The guidance shapes decisions by acting as a tie-breaker. When the real-time decision is ambiguous—should I flip the light now or wait two more seconds?—the cached guidance says: my neighbor sent a prediction that they need priority soon. So the real-time process follows the guidance. This makes intersections coordinate without blocking each other because each light reads a cached neighbor forecast instead of waiting for a new conversation.

Reinforcement learning trains the LLM to send good guidance and adjust reasoning depth. If an intersection's guidance consistently makes the network slower, the reward signal drops, and the LLM learns to either predict differently or focus reasoning on the neighbors that actually matter. Chunk-count penalties prevent reasoning from bloating because extra words lower the reward when they do not improve throughput.

stages.s: Current traffic at this intersection and all neighbors
Asynchronous reasoning: predict neighbor arrivals for next 30 seconds
Real-time: read cached guidance in real-time decision loop
Adjust green duration based on neighbor guidance
Signal timing that coordinates with neighbors

math.words: Each intersection receives a cooperation signal from each neighbor. That signal is the sum of a traffic prediction and a reasoning cost penalty. The traffic prediction predicts how many vehicles will arrive at this intersection from that neighbor in the next time window. The reasoning cost is how many tokens and computation steps it took to make that prediction. The final guidance weight trades off prediction accuracy against reasoning budget.
math.equation: G_ij = Pred_ij - beta * Cost_ij   where Cost_ij = alpha * (tokens_used + computation_steps)
symbols: guidance quality from intersection i to intersection j
prediction of vehicles arriving at j from i
trade-off: how much to penalize extra reasoning cost
reasoning cost in tokens and steps
scaling factor to make cost comparable to prediction magnitude
number of tokens the LLM generated for this prediction
number of forward passes through the model

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Intersection A reasons about Intersection B. Prediction: 45 vehicles will arrive in 30 seconds.
The reasoning used 200 chunks of text and 8 forward passes. Cost = 1.0 * (200 + 8) = 208.
Guidance to B is 24.2. Intersection B's real-time signal reads this: there is moderate but confident help coming from A.
If reasoning had used only 50 chunks of text (faster model), Cost = 50, G_AB = 45 - 5 = 40. B receives stronger guidance. So faster thinking is rewarded.

math.note: The formula shows the core trade-off: good predictions help the network because lights can prepare for incoming cars, but computing them costs chunks of text. Training learns the right beta to balance speed and accuracy.

items.html: If the cached prediction is old, it may not match current traffic. A sudden accident upstream changes the flow, but the real-time decision is still reading yesterday's guidance. The paper uses time stamps and adaptive cache invalidation to address this: guidance older than a few seconds is discarded.

items.b: Reasoning cost spirals out of control.
items.html: The LLM might use 5000 chunks of text to predict traffic a minute away, when 200 chunks of text would have given almost as good a guess. Without the cost penalty in the reward function, the model wastes computation. The reinforcement learning reward must penalize chunk of text bloat.

items.b: Circular dependency: A waits for B, B waits for A.
items.html: If two intersections send guidance that contradicts each other, the real-time decisions deadlock. The paper avoids this by making the real-time decision layer never fully trust guidance—it reads cached guidance as a hint, not a command. Local urgency (long queue at this intersection) always overrides guidance.

items.b: Done right: guidance is a suggestion, not a law.
items.html: The real-time decision uses guidance to break ties, but if this intersection's own queue is urgent, it acts on the local need. This ensures the network never deadlocks and always keeps intersections moving.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small network of three to five intersections. Simulate arriving cars with realistic patterns: morning rush (more cars arrive west-bound), midday, evening (more cars exit the downtown). Run two versions side by side: (1) isolated LLM agents at each intersection, each deciding alone; (2) CoLLMLight with asynchronous cooperation. Measure the total time all cars spend waiting in queues.
demo.metric_eq: total_wait_time = sum over all cars of (time_car_entered_queue_to_time_car_left_queue); compare isolated vs cooperative
demo.closing: The demo should make it impossible to miss that cooperation reduces total wait time, and that this improvement comes from intersections sending each other traffic predictions asynchronously, not from increasing the latency of real-time decisions.
